title: Classification, Monera and Viruses

toc.title: 2.1 Classification systems, taxonomic hierarchy and binomial nomenclature

html:
Biodiversity is the heaviest unit of the Botany section — 9 of the 40 questions — and this first chapter of it carries about 2. The questions are built from a short list: who proposed which system and on what basis, the order of the taxonomic ranks, the rules of binomial nomenclature, the parts of a bacterial cell, Gram staining, the modes of bacterial nutrition, the phases of the growth curve, the special features of cyanobacteria (heterocysts, phycocyanin), and the structure and chemistry of viruses (TMV and the T4 phage).

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Systems and their authors — two kingdoms (Linnaeus, 1758), five kingdoms (Whittaker, 1969), three domains (Woese, 1990, on rRNA sequences).
  • Hierarchy and naming — kingdom → division → class → order → family → genus → species; the rules of binomial nomenclature (italics, capitals, no tautonyms in plants).
  • Bacterial cell — peptidoglycan wall, 70S ribosomes, nucleoid, plasmid, mesosome, flagellar arrangements; Gram-positive vs Gram-negative.
  • Nutrition and growth — photo- and chemoautotrophs with examples; the lag, log, stationary and decline phases; N = N_0 \times 2^n.
  • Cyanobacteria — oxygenic photosynthesis with chlorophyll a and phycobilins, heterocysts for nitrogen fixation, no flagella.
  • Viruses — DNA or RNA but never both, capsid of capsomeres, helical (TMV), polyhedral and complex (T4) symmetry; viroids and prions.

2.1 Classification systems, taxonomic hierarchy and binomial nomenclature

Taxonomy is the science of identifying, naming and classifying organisms (the word was coined by A. P. de Candolle, 1813); systematics adds their evolutionary relationships. A taxon is a group of any rank — a species, a family, a kingdom.

From two kingdoms to three domains

System Proposed by Groups Basis / what it fixed
Two kingdoms Carolus Linnaeus (1758) Plantae, Animalia presence of a cell wall and photosynthesis vs locomotion and ingestion
Three kingdoms Ernst Haeckel (1866) + Protista unicellular forms separated
Four kingdoms H. F. Copeland (1956) Monera, Protista, Plantae, Animalia prokaryotes separated
Five kingdoms R. H. Whittaker (1969) Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction, phylogeny
Six kingdoms Carl Woese (1977) Monera split into Archaebacteria and Eubacteria rRNA differences
Three domains Carl Woese, O. Kandler and M. Wheelis (1990) Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya (above kingdoms) sequences of 16S/18S ribosomal RNA

Why two kingdoms failed. It put prokaryotes (bacteria, blue-green algae) and eukaryotes in one kingdom; it lumped heterotrophic fungi, which have chitin walls, with green plants; it lumped unicellular and multicellular forms together; and it had no place for Euglena (green, yet wall-less and able to feed like an animal), slime moulds (an animal-like feeding stage and a plant-like spore stage), lichens and viruses.

Feature Monera Protista Fungi Plantae Animalia
Cell type prokaryotic eukaryotic eukaryotic eukaryotic eukaryotic
Cell wall non-cellulosic (peptidoglycan) present in some present, chitin present, cellulose absent
Nuclear membrane absent present present present present
Body organisation cellular cellular (unicellular) multicellular or loose tissue tissue and organ tissue, organ and organ system
Nutrition autotrophic (photo- or chemosynthetic) and heterotrophic photosynthetic and heterotrophic heterotrophic (absorptive — saprophytic, parasitic) autotrophic (photosynthetic) heterotrophic (holozoic)
Examples bacteria, cyanobacteria, Mycoplasma diatoms, dinoflagellates, Euglena, slime moulds, Amoeba yeast, Mucor, Agaricus, Penicillium algae, mosses, ferns, pines, flowering plants Hydra, earthworm, frog, humans
What stays outside the five kingdoms

Whittaker's scheme has no place for viruses, viroids, prions and lichens — they are discussed separately. A question that offers "Monera" as the kingdom of viruses is a trap: viruses are acellular.

Feature Archaea Bacteria Eukarya
Nuclear envelope absent absent present
Peptidoglycan in wall absent (some have pseudomurein) present absent
Membrane lipids ether-linked, branched chains ester-linked, unbranched ester-linked, unbranched
Histones present in some absent present
First amino acid of a protein methionine formyl-methionine methionine
Growth inhibited by streptomycin, chloramphenicol no yes no
Ribosomes 70S 70S 80S (70S in organelles)

Archaea live in extreme habitats: methanogens (Methanobacterium, in marshes and the rumen of cattle — they make the methane of biogas/gobar-gas plants), halophiles (Halobacterium, in salt lakes) and thermoacidophiles (Sulfolobus, Thermoplasma, in hot sulphur springs).

Taxonomic hierarchy

Linnaeus arranged the ranks in a fixed order, the taxonomic hierarchy. Moving up from species to kingdom, each rank contains more organisms that share fewer characters. Species is the basic unit: a group of similar individuals that interbreed in nature to give fertile offspring and are reproductively isolated from other such groups (Ernst Mayr's biological species concept, 1942; the word "species" was first used by John Ray).

Rank Ending in plants Mango Wheat Human
Kingdom — Plantae Plantae Animalia
Division (plants) / Phylum (animals) -phyta Angiospermae Angiospermae Chordata
Class -opsida, -phyceae (algae), -mycetes (fungi) Dicotyledonae Monocotyledonae Mammalia
Order -ales Sapindales Poales Primata
Family -aceae Anacardiaceae Poaceae Hominidae
Genus — Mangifera Triticum Homo
Species — indica aestivum sapiens
The ranks, top to bottom

"King David Came Over For Good Soup" — Kingdom, Division, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. (Animals: Phylum for Division.)

Binomial nomenclature

Every species has a two-word scientific name: the generic name followed by the specific epithet. Gaspard Bauhin used two-word names (1623), but Linnaeus made the system universal in Species Plantarum (1753) for plants and Systema Naturae (10th edition, 1758) for animals. Plant names are governed by the ICN (International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi and plants, formerly ICBN), animal names by the ICZN, bacteria by the ICNP and viruses by the ICTV.

  1. Names are in Latin or are Latinised, whatever their origin.
  2. The generic name starts with a capital letter; the specific epithet is all small letters — Rhododendron arboreum (lali gurans), Azadirachta indica (neem).
  3. Printed names are in italics; handwritten names are underlined, each word separately.
  4. The author's name may follow in roman type, often abbreviated: Mangifera indica L. (L. = Linnaeus).
  5. Priority: the earliest validly published name is the correct one (for plants, counted from 1 May 1753).
  6. Tautonyms (genus and species the same word) are not allowed in plants, though zoology allows them — Naja naja (cobra), Rattus rattus.
  7. A subspecies or variety gives a trinomial — Homo sapiens sapiens.

2.2 Bacteria and cyanobacteria

Shapes and the bacterial cell

Bacteria were first seen by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1676), who called them "animalcules". Most are 0.5–5 μm long; Mycoplasma (0.1–0.3 μm, no cell wall, unaffected by penicillin) is the smallest free-living cell.

Shape Name Arrangements and examples
Spherical coccus diplococcus (pairs: Streptococcus pneumoniae), streptococcus (chains), staphylococcus (grape-like bunches: Staphylococcus aureus), tetrad (4), sarcina (cube of 8)
Rod bacillus single (Bacillus, E. coli), streptobacillus (chain)
Comma vibrio Vibrio cholerae
Rigid spiral spirillum Spirillum
Flexible spiral spirochaete Treponema pallidum (syphilis)

Structure Facts the paper asks
Glycocalyx a loose slime layer or a firm capsule; the capsule protects from phagocytes and makes Streptococcus pneumoniae virulent (Griffith's S strain)
Cell wall rigid peptidoglycan (murein) — chains of N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM) cross-linked by short peptides; penicillin blocks the cross-linking
Plasma membrane phospholipid bilayer without sterols; carries the respiratory enzymes (there are no mitochondria)
Mesosome infolding of the membrane; helps in wall formation, DNA replication and distribution to daughter cells, respiration and secretion
Nucleoid one circular double-stranded DNA molecule, without a nuclear membrane or true histones
Plasmid small circular extra-chromosomal DNA that replicates on its own; carries genes such as antibiotic resistance (R plasmid) or fertility (F plasmid); used as a cloning vector
Ribosomes 70S (50S + 30S)
Inclusions glycogen, poly-β-hydroxybutyrate, volutin (polyphosphate) granules; gas vacuoles in aquatic forms
Flagellum a single hollow fibril of the protein flagellin, without the 9 + 2 pattern; it rotates
Pili and fimbriae sex pili (pilin) transfer DNA in conjugation; fimbriae attach cells to surfaces
Endospore thick-walled resting body of Bacillus and Clostridium, rich in calcium dipicolinate; survives boiling

Flagellar arrangements: atrichous (none), monotrichous (one at one end — Vibrio cholerae), lophotrichous (a tuft at one end — Pseudomonas fluorescens), amphitrichous (at both ends — Spirillum), peritrichous (all over the surface — E. coli, Salmonella typhi).

Gram staining

Hans Christian Gram (1884): stain with crystal violet → fix with iodine (mordant) → wash with alcohol (decolouriser) → counterstain with safranin. Gram-positive cells stay violet; Gram-negative cells lose the violet and take up the pink-red safranin.

Feature Gram-positive Gram-negative
Peptidoglycan thick (20–80 nm), many layers thin (2–7 nm), one or two layers
Teichoic acids present absent
Outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) absent present
Periplasmic space absent or very small present
Sensitivity to penicillin high lower
Examples Bacillus, Clostridium, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Lactobacillus E. coli, Salmonella, Vibrio, Pseudomonas, Rhizobium, Azotobacter, cyanobacteria

Nutrition

Mode Source of energy and carbon Examples
Photoautotrophic (anoxygenic) light; H₂S or organic acids as H donor, so no O₂ is released; bacteriochlorophyll green sulphur (Chlorobium), purple sulphur (Chromatium), purple non-sulphur (Rhodospirillum) bacteria
Photoautotrophic (oxygenic) light; H₂O is split, O₂ released; chlorophyll a cyanobacteria
Chemoautotrophic energy from oxidising inorganic substances; CO₂ fixed Nitrosomonas (NH₃ → NO₂⁻), Nitrobacter (NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻), Thiobacillus and Beggiatoa (H₂S → S → SO₄²⁻), iron bacteria (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺)
Saprophytic dead organic matter Bacillus, Clostridium, Pseudomonas — decomposers
Parasitic living host, causing disease Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Vibrio cholerae, Xanthomonas
Symbiotic living host, mutual benefit Rhizobium in legume root nodules; E. coli in the colon (makes vitamin K)

Anoxygenic photosynthesis by a green sulphur bacterium: 6CO₂ + 12H₂S → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 12S. Sulphur, not oxygen, is the by-product.

Reproduction and growth

Bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission — the DNA replicates, the cell elongates and a septum divides it into two identical cells. It is amitotic: no spindle, no chromosome condensation. Under ideal conditions E. coli divides every 20 minutes. Endospores help survival, not multiplication (one cell → one spore → one cell). There is no true sexual reproduction, but genes are recombined by transformation (uptake of free DNA; Griffith, 1928), conjugation (transfer through a sex pilus; Lederberg and Tatum, 1946) and transduction (transfer by a bacteriophage; Zinder and Lederberg, 1952).

Bacterial growth means an increase in the number of cells. In the log phase the number doubles every generation, so after n generations

N = N_0 \times 2^{n}, \qquad n = \frac{t}{g} = \frac{\log N - \log N_0}{\log 2}

where N_0 is the starting number, t the time and g the generation (doubling) time.

Phase What happens
Lag cells adapt to the new medium, grow in size and make enzymes; numbers hardly change
Log (exponential) division at the maximum constant rate; generation time is shortest; cells are most uniform and most sensitive to antibiotics
Stationary nutrients run out and wastes build up; division rate = death rate; secondary metabolites (antibiotics) and endospores are formed
Decline (death) deaths exceed divisions; numbers fall exponentially

Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae)

Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes of the kingdom Monera, about 3.5 billion years old (stromatolites); their oxygen built up Earth's atmosphere, and a cyanobacterium engulfed by an early eukaryote became the chloroplast.

  • Cell: prokaryotic, with a Gram-negative-type peptidoglycan wall, usually inside a mucilage sheath; no nucleus, no chloroplast, no mitochondria.
  • Pigments: chlorophyll a (no chlorophyll b), carotenoids, and the phycobilins — c-phycocyanin (blue) and c-phycoerythrin (red) — held in phycobilisomes on free thylakoids. The blend gives the blue-green colour.
  • Photosynthesis is oxygenic, with both photosystems, like green plants.
  • Reserve food: cyanophycean starch (glycogen-like) and cyanophycin (protein) granules.
  • No flagella at any stage; some filaments glide or oscillate (Oscillatoria).
  • Gas vacuoles (pseudovacuoles) keep planktonic forms afloat.
  • Heterocysts: large, pale, thick-walled cells of Nostoc and Anabaena that fix nitrogen. They lack photosystem II, so they make no O₂ that would destroy nitrogenase.
  • Reproduction: only vegetative and asexual — fission, fragmentation into hormogonia, and thick-walled resting akinetes. No sexual reproduction and no motile cells.
  • Forms: unicellular (Chroococcus), colonial (Gloeocapsa, Microcystis), filamentous (Oscillatoria, Nostoc, Anabaena, Spirulina).
  • Importance: nitrogen fixation in rice fields (Anabaena, Nostoc, Aulosira); Anabaena azollae inside the water fern Azolla (biofertiliser); Nostoc as the partner of many lichens and in the coralloid roots of Cycas; Spirulina as protein-rich single-cell protein; Microcystis forms toxic water blooms.
"Blue-green algae" are not algae

Algae are eukaryotes with chloroplasts. Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes in Monera. Options that give them "chlorophyll b", "a nucleus", "flagellated zoospores" or "sexual reproduction by gametes" are all wrong.

2.3 Viruses

Discovery and characteristics

Year Scientist Discovery
1892 Dmitri Ivanowsky sap of mosaic-diseased tobacco stays infectious after passing a bacteria-proof filter
1898 M. W. Beijerinck called the agent "contagium vivum fluidum" (contagious living fluid); named it virus
1898 Loeffler and Frosch foot-and-mouth disease virus — the first animal virus
1915–17 F. W. Twort, F. d'Hérelle bacteriophages — viruses of bacteria
1935 W. M. Stanley crystallised TMV (Nobel Prize 1946)
1936 Bawden and Pirie TMV is a nucleoprotein (protein + RNA)
1971 T. O. Diener viroids — potato spindle tuber disease
1982 Stanley Prusiner prions — infectious proteins (Nobel Prize 1997)

A virus is an acellular, ultramicroscopic (about 20–300 nm), obligate intracellular parasite made of nucleic acid in a protein coat. It has no metabolism of its own and multiplies only inside a living host cell, using the host's ribosomes, enzymes and energy.

Like non-living things Like living things
no cell, cytoplasm or cell membrane possess genetic material (DNA or RNA)
no metabolism, respiration or growth outside a host multiply inside a host and pass on their characters
can be crystallised and stored like chemicals mutate and evolve
inert outside the host infect specific hosts and cause disease

Structure and chemical composition

  • The complete infectious particle is the virion.
  • Capsid — the protein coat, built of identical subunits called capsomeres; it protects the nucleic acid and decides the host by attaching to it. Capsid + nucleic acid = nucleocapsid.
  • Nucleic acid — DNA or RNA, never both; single- or double-stranded, linear or circular. It is the infective part.
  • Envelope — present in some viruses (HIV, influenza, herpes, SARS-CoV-2): a lipid bilayer taken from the host membrane, studded with viral glycoprotein spikes (peplomers). Viruses without it are naked (TMV, adenovirus, poliovirus, most phages).
  • Enzymes in some: reverse transcriptase in retroviruses (HIV); lysozyme in the tail of T4; neuraminidase in influenza.

Chemically, a virus is mostly protein: TMV is about 95 % protein and 5 % RNA.

Feature Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) T4 bacteriophage
Host tobacco (plant) Escherichia coli (bacterium)
Shape and symmetry rigid rod, about 300 × 18 nm; helical tadpole-like; complex — polyhedral head + helical tail
Nucleic acid single-stranded RNA, about 6400 nucleotides, coiled helically inside the capsid double-stranded DNA, linear, packed in the head
Capsid 2130 identical capsomeres, each binding 3 nucleotides head, collar, contractile tail sheath round a hollow core, base plate with six tail fibres
Envelope none none

Types of viruses

Basis Types and examples
Host plant viruses — mostly ssRNA (TMV, potato virus X; cauliflower mosaic virus is dsDNA); animal viruses — DNA or RNA (polio, influenza, HIV, herpes, pox); bacteriophages — mostly dsDNA (T2, T4, λ; φX174 has ssDNA); mycophages (fungi) and cyanophages
Nucleic acid dsDNA (T4, pox, herpes, adenovirus, hepatitis B); ssDNA (φX174, parvovirus); dsRNA (reovirus, rotavirus, wound tumour virus of plants); ssRNA (TMV, polio, influenza, HIV, SARS-CoV-2)
Symmetry helical (TMV, influenza nucleocapsid); polyhedral / icosahedral — 20 triangular faces (adenovirus, poliovirus, herpes); complex (T4 phage, poxvirus)
Envelope enveloped (HIV, influenza, herpes) or naked (TMV, adenovirus, polio)
Life cycle (phages) virulent — lytic cycle only, the host bursts (T4); temperate — can also integrate into the host DNA as a prophage and be copied silently (lysogenic cycle; λ phage)

Sub-viral agents. Viroids are tiny, naked, circular single-stranded RNA molecules (about 250–400 nucleotides) with no protein coat that infect plants (potato spindle tuber, citrus exocortis). Prions are infectious proteins with no nucleic acid that cause scrapie in sheep, mad cow disease (BSE) and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease in humans.

Eliminating options on viruses

If an option gives a virus both DNA and RNA, ribosomes, a cell wall, independent metabolism, or sensitivity to penicillin — strike it out. If it calls a virus a member of Monera — strike it out. (Some question banks claim that the "leukoviruses" contain both; they are retroviruses whose genome is RNA, copied into DNA only inside the host cell.)

Bacterial exponential growth and generation count

Problem. An Escherichia coli culture with a doubling time of 20 minutes starts with 5 \times 10^3 cells mL^{-1}. How many cells mL^{-1} are present after 2 hours of log-phase growth?

Solution. Two hours = 120 minutes gives n = 120 / 20 = 6 generations. Therefore N = N_0 \times 2^n = 5 \times 10^3 \times 2^6 = 5 \times 10^3 \times 64 = \mathbf{3.2 \times 10^5\text{ cells mL}^{-1}}.

Decoding viral nucleic acid type from base composition

Problem. Chemical analysis of a purified plant virus reveals 28 % adenine, 22 % uracil, 26 % guanine, and 24 % cytosine. What type of genome does this virus possess?

Solution. The presence of uracil (and absence of thymine) proves the genome is RNA. Because A \neq U (28 % vs 22 %) and G \neq C (26 % vs 24 %), Chargaff's base-pairing equality fails, so the genome is single-stranded RNA (ssRNA), typical of TMV.

Gram stain outcome and cell-wall chemistry

Problem. During a Gram-staining practical, a student forgets the iodine mordant step and proceeds straight from crystal violet to ethanol decolourisation and safranin counterstain. How will Staphylococcus aureus (a Gram-positive coccus) appear?

Solution. Without Gram's iodine (\text{I}_2\text{/KI}), the large crystal-violet–iodine (CV–I) complex never forms inside the thick peptidoglycan mesh. Ethanol washes the uncomplexed crystal violet out, and safranin stains the cells pink/red (a false Gram-negative result).

Chapter summary

  • Linnaeus (1758) gave two kingdoms; Whittaker (1969) gave five — Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — chiefly on cell structure, body organisation and mode of nutrition; Woese (1990) placed three domains — Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya — above them, on rRNA sequences.
  • The hierarchy runs kingdom, division, class, order (-ales), family (-aceae), genus, species; species is the basic unit.
  • Binomial names (Linnaeus, 1753): Latin, genus capitalised, epithet small, italicised or underlined separately; tautonyms are not allowed in plants.
  • Bacteria have a peptidoglycan wall, 70S ribosomes, a nucleoid and often plasmids; they are cocci, bacilli, vibrios or spirilla.
  • Gram-positive walls have thick peptidoglycan and stay violet; Gram-negative walls are thin with an outer lipopolysaccharide membrane and stain pink.
  • Bacteria are photoautotrophic (anoxygenic, except cyanobacteria), chemoautotrophic (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), saprophytic, parasitic or symbiotic.
  • Binary fission doubles the population each generation (N = N_0 \times 2^n); the growth curve has lag, log, stationary and decline phases.
  • Cyanobacteria are oxygenic prokaryotes with chlorophyll a and phycobilins, cyanophycean starch, heterocysts for N₂ fixation, and no flagella or sexual reproduction.
  • Viruses are acellular obligate parasites with DNA or RNA (never both) in a protein capsid; TMV is a helical ssRNA rod, T4 a complex dsDNA phage.
  • Viroids are naked RNA; prions are infectious proteins.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (b) — Whittaker (1969) added Fungi as a kingdom beside Monera, Protista, Plantae and Animalia. Woese gave the three domains; Linnaeus two kingdoms; Haeckel added Protista.

2. (d) — Woese compared 16S/18S rRNA sequences and found archaea as different from bacteria as from eukaryotes.

3. (a) — The order is kingdom, division, class, order, family, genus, species.

4. (c) — Genus with a capital, specific epithet in small letters, both in italics when printed.

5. (a) — Tautonyms (genus and species the same word) are forbidden by the ICN but allowed in zoology (Naja naja).

6. (b) — Archaeal walls lack peptidoglycan (some have pseudomurein). Cyanobacteria have a Gram-negative-type peptidoglycan wall.

7. (d) — Methanogens are archaea with ether-linked membrane lipids; they produce methane in marshes, the rumen and biogas plants.

8. (c) — Vibrios are comma-shaped, e.g. Vibrio cholerae. Spirilla are rigid spirals.

9. (b) — Peritrichous (E. coli, Salmonella); monotrichous is one flagellum at one end, lophotrichous a tuft at one end.

10. (a) — Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S (50S + 30S); 80S ribosomes are in the eukaryotic cytoplasm.

11. (c) — Plasmids are extra-chromosomal, self-replicating circular DNA. Option (b) is the mesosome; option (d) volutin.

12. (d) — Safranin stains the decolourised Gram-negative cells pink. Crystal violet is the primary stain, iodine the mordant, alcohol the decolouriser.

13. (a) — Nitrosomonas oxidises NH₃ (NH₄⁺) to NO₂⁻; Nitrobacter then oxidises NO₂⁻ to NO₃⁻.

14. (d) — In the log (exponential) phase the generation time is shortest and constant. In the lag phase cells adapt; in the stationary phase division equals death.

15. (b) — Heterocysts lack photosystem II and have thick walls, so nitrogenase is protected from O₂. Akinetes are resting spores; hormogonia are fragments for propagation.

16. (c) — c-Phycocyanin is the blue phycobilin. Cyanobacteria lack chlorophyll b; fucoxanthin is the pigment of brown algae.

17. (d) — Beijerinck (1898) called it a contagious living fluid. Ivanowsky (1892) first showed it passes bacteria-proof filters; Stanley crystallised TMV in 1935.

18. (a) — A virus has a genome of DNA or of RNA, not both. Many are DNA viruses (T4, pox) and many RNA viruses (TMV, HIV).

19. (c) — The capsid is made of capsomeres. The envelope is the extra lipid layer of some viruses; peplomers are its spikes.

20. (b) — TMV is a rigid rod of 2130 capsomeres wound helically round single-stranded RNA.

Set B — Understanding (12 questions)

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (d) — Euglena photosynthesises like a plant but has no wall and can absorb food like an animal, so it fits neither kingdom. It is eukaryotic and has no chitin.

2. (b) — Fungi lack chlorophyll, absorb food from outside, and have chitin walls — nutrition was a key criterion for Whittaker. They are eukaryotic, and most are multicellular.

3. (a) — Archaea, like eukaryotes, start proteins with methionine and have histones; bacteria use formyl-methionine. Archaea still have 70S ribosomes and no nucleus.

4. (c) — Alcohol dissolves the outer lipid membrane and the thin peptidoglycan cannot hold the dye–iodine complex. Option (a) describes Gram-positive walls, which keep the stain.

5. (b) — Penicillin blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in a growing wall; Mycoplasma has no wall to attack.

6. (d) — Reproduction must increase the number of individuals; an endospore is only a survival stage. It germinates readily under good conditions.

7. (c) — Cyanobacteria have both photosystems and split H₂O, releasing O₂ (oxygenic). Sulphur bacteria use H₂S and release sulphur instead (anoxygenic).

8. (a) — Nitrogenase is destroyed by O₂. Heterocysts lack PS II (no water splitting) and have thick walls that slow O₂ entry. Leghaemoglobin protects nitrogenase in legume nodules, not in heterocysts.

9. (d) — Reproduction with inheritance and mutation are properties of life. Crystallisation and lack of metabolism are non-living features.

10. (a) — Antibacterial drugs attack walls, 70S ribosomes or bacterial enzymes; a virus uses the host's machinery, so there is no target. Many viruses are naked, so (c) is false.

11. (c) — Uracil without thymine means RNA; influenza is an enveloped ssRNA virus. T4, adenovirus and cauliflower mosaic virus are all naked DNA viruses.

12. (b) — Viroids (Diener, 1971) are naked circular ssRNA. Option (c) describes prions.

Answers and explanations — Set C

1. (c) — n = 120 min ÷ 20 min = 6 generations; N = 100 × 2⁶ = 100 × 64 = 6400. Option (a) adds instead of doubling; (d) counts seven generations.

2. (a) — 1 024 000 ÷ 1000 = 1024 = 2¹⁰, so 10 generations in 300 minutes: g = 300 ÷ 10 = 30 minutes.

3. (d) — Handwritten binomials are underlined, each word separately, with the genus capitalised and the epithet in small letters.

4. (b) — Pink after Gram's stain means Gram-negative; rod-shaped is a bacillus; flagella all over is peritrichous — Salmonella typhi.

5. (a) — Prokaryotic with a peptidoglycan wall means Monera; chlorophyll a with O₂ release marks a cyanobacterium. Algae with chloroplasts would be eukaryotes.

6. (c) — Destroyed by RNase (so RNA), unharmed by protease and without a coat: a viroid, as in potato spindle tuber disease. Prions are protein and would be destroyed by protease.

7. (d) — Energy comes from oxidising NH₄⁺ to NO₂⁻ without light, and carbon from CO₂: a chemoautotroph such as Nitrosomonas.

8. (b) — 6400 ÷ 2130 ≈ 3. Each TMV coat-protein subunit binds three nucleotides of the RNA helix.
